new.title: Stand in for a Beatle on Beatles-Platz
new.desc: Where the Reeperbahn meets Große Freiheit, steel silhouettes of the band stand on a square paved like a vinyl record, a few steps from the clubs where they learned their trade.
new.tip: Come after dark when the record lights up, then walk up Große Freiheit past the Kaiserkeller and the Indra.

new.title: Climb the green bunker on Feldstraße
new.desc: The huge wartime Flakturm IV on the Heiligengeistfeld got five extra storeys and a rooftop garden in 2024. A planted Bergpfad (mountain path) winds around the concrete to the top.
new.tip: Walk up the outside path for a view over the Millerntor stadium and the harbour cranes. U3 Feldstraße is right at the foot.

new.title: See the Rote Flora on Schulterblatt
new.desc: This graffiti-covered former theatre has been squatted since 1989 and is still the stubborn heart of the left-wing Schanzenviertel.
new.tip: Grab a seat on the Piazza opposite, the row of Portuguese and Spanish cafés, and watch the Schanze go by.

new.title: Watch the sun set under Park Fiction's palms
new.desc: Neighbours fought for this little park above the Elbe and designed it themselves, steel palm trees included. It is the St. Pauli spot for watching container ships at dusk.
new.tip: Bring a drink from a kiosk on the way and sit on the lawn facing the docks.

new.title: Take the 136 steps up the Dockland
new.desc: This glass office building leans out over the Elbe like a ship's bow, and its outside staircase leads to a public roof deck above the fishing harbour.
new.tip: The harbour ferry stops right beside it (Dockland Fischereihafen), so combine it with a ride along the river.

new.title: Look over the port from the Altonaer Balkon
new.desc: A green terrace on the high Elbe bank behind Altona's white town hall, with a wide view of the container terminals and the river traffic.
new.tip: Locals come with a picnic at the end of the day. Altona station is a ten minute walk.

new.title: Wander the Museumshafen Oevelgönne
new.desc: Old Elbe sailing barges, a steam icebreaker, a lightship and a retired harbour ferry are moored here, all kept afloat by volunteers.
new.tip: The pontoons are open to walk on. Arrive by harbour ferry 62 to Neumühlen/Oevelgönne, then carry on along the beach.

new.title: Stroll down Jenischpark to the Elbe
new.desc: Hamburg's oldest landscaped park rolls from the white Jenisch Haus down towards the river, with ancient oaks and the wild little Flottbek valley cutting through it.
new.tip: The Ernst Barlach Haus in the park is a quiet stop on a wet day. S1 to Klein Flottbek, then walk south.

new.title: Get lost in the Loki Schmidt Garten
new.desc: The university's botanical garden in Klein Flottbek is laid out in themed gardens from around the world and costs nothing to enter.
new.tip: It sits right next to S-Bahn Klein Flottbek, so pair it with Jenischpark across the road.

new.title: Walk among angels at Friedhof Ohlsdorf
new.desc: The largest park cemetery in the world is closer to a forest than a graveyard: ponds, chapels, mausoleums of shipping dynasties and the graves of many famous Hamburgers.
new.tip: It is so big that two city bus lines run through it. Come between late April and early June when the rhododendrons bloom.
new.q: Friedhof Ohlsdorf Haupteingang, Fuhlsbüttler Straße, Hamburg

new.title: See stars in the Stadtpark water tower
new.desc: The brick water tower at the end of the Stadtpark's great lawn has been a planetarium since 1930, with a big dome for shows and a viewing platform 45 metres up.
new.tip: Shows sell out at weekends, so book ahead. The platform looks straight down the park's main axis to the lake.

new.title: Follow the emigrants at BallinStadt
new.desc: Around five million Europeans passed through Hamburg on their way to the Americas. The rebuilt emigrant halls on Veddel tell their stories on the very spot where they waited for their ship.
new.tip: The S-Bahn stop Veddel (BallinStadt) is a short walk away. Allow a couple of hours.

new.title: Watch the tide in the Heuckenlock forest
new.desc: At the southern tip of Wilhelmsburg lies one of Europe's last freshwater tidal forests. The Elbe floods it around a hundred times a year and sea eagles nest in the trees.
new.tip: From the bridge on the trail you can see the creek fill and empty. Check the water level first, as the path goes under at high tide.

new.title: Eat a Fischbrötchen at the Sunday Fischmarkt
new.desc: Since 1703 Altona's fish market has been allowed to trade on Sunday mornings. Today night owls and early birds meet between shouting stallholders, fruit baskets and fish rolls.
new.tip: It is over by mid-morning and starts later in winter. Afterwards, follow the live music into the old Fischauktionshalle.

new.title: Snack your way round the St. Pauli Nachtmarkt
new.desc: Every Wednesday the Spielbudenplatz, in the middle of the Reeperbahn, turns into an evening market with food stalls, drinks and neighbours doing their shopping.
new.tip: It runs from late afternoon into the evening, which makes it an easy start to a night on the Kiez.

new.title: Graze along the Isemarkt under the U-Bahn
new.desc: More than 200 stalls line up for about 750 metres beneath the iron viaduct of the U3, so the market stays dry in any weather. Regional produce, cheese, fish and plenty to eat on the spot.
new.tip: Tuesday and Friday mornings only. Start at Hoheluftbrücke station and eat your way to Eppendorfer Baum.

new.title: Have a beer in the sand at Strandperle
new.desc: The original Elbe beach kiosk at Övelgönne: feet in the sand, drink in hand, and container ships gliding past almost close enough to touch.
new.tip: Walk west along the beach from the Museumshafen. Sunny evenings get crowded, so come early.

new.title: Toast the sunset at the Alsterperle
new.desc: A tiny beer garden kiosk right on the east shore of the Außenalster, where half of Uhlenhorst gathers to watch sailing boats and the evening light over the city spires.
new.tip: Evenings are best. Walk or cycle there along the lakeside path through the Alsterpark.

new.title: Order cake by canoe at Café Canale
new.desc: This basement café in a Jugendstil house in Winterhude sits right on the Mühlenkampkanal and hands coffee and Blechkuchen (tray-baked fruit cake) through a window to passing paddlers.
new.tip: Hire a canoe or pedal boat nearby and pull up at the window. On foot, the entrance is on Poelchaukamp.

new.title: Try a Franzbrötchen from Kleine Konditorei
new.desc: The Franzbrötchen, a squashed, sticky cinnamon and butter pastry, is Hamburg's own breakfast. Locals rate this Eimsbüttel bakery as one of the best places in town to get one.
new.tip: Go in the morning while they are still warm, then stroll along Osterstraße, Eimsbüttel's high street.

new.title: Eat in the old cattle halls at Bullerei
new.desc: A big, buzzy restaurant in the former livestock halls beside Sternschanze station, known for its meat and for a relaxed deli side that is easier on the wallet.
new.tip: Reserve for the restaurant in the evening. The deli usually has room at lunchtime without booking.

new.title: Warm up with scones at Lühmanns Teestube
new.desc: For almost forty years this Blankenese tea room has served home-baked cakes, scones and pots of tea to walkers coming up from the Elbe beach.
new.tip: It is a few minutes from S-Bahn Blankenese, ideal after the stairs of the Treppenviertel. Closed early in the week.

new.title: Drink above a boxing ring at Zur Ritze
new.desc: A Reeperbahn institution with walls covered in photos of boxers and Kiez characters, and a real boxing ring in the cellar where champions have trained.
new.tip: The entrance is in a courtyard off Reeperbahn 140. Go for one beer and a look around rather than a long night.

new.title: Hear Hells Bells at the Millerntor
new.desc: FC St. Pauli's stadium is mostly standing terraces and all attitude. The team walks out to AC/DC's Hells Bells and every home goal is met with Blur's Song 2.
new.tip: Tickets go fast, so watch the club's official resale. Be inside early, as the fans insist on time to sing before kick-off.

new.title: Ride the big wheel at the Hamburger Dom
new.desc: Northern Germany's biggest funfair fills the Heiligengeistfeld three times a year, each time for about a month, with rides, Schmalzkuchen and a lot of neon.
new.tip: Friday nights end with fireworks. U3 St. Pauli and Feldstraße both stop right at an entrance.

new.title: Catch a band where the Beatles started
new.desc: In August 1960 an unknown Liverpool band played their first Hamburg shows at the Indra on Große Freiheit. It is still a small live club with rock 'n' roll, blues, soul and jam sessions.
new.tip: Check the club's programme before you go, as it does not open every night.

new.title: Go vintage hunting on Marktstraße
new.desc: The main street of the Karoviertel is a run of small designers, record shops and second-hand stores such as Hot Dogs, with cafés in between.
new.tip: Shops open late in the morning. Saturday afternoon is liveliest, and the green bunker is just around the corner.

new.title: Climb the stairs of Blankenese
new.desc: The old fishing village of Blankenese tumbles down a steep hill to the Elbe. Nearly five thousand steps thread between captains' cottages, gardens and sudden river views.
new.tip: Walk down to the Strandweg and its beach, then let the small local bus, nicknamed the Bergziege (mountain goat), carry you back up to the S-Bahn.

new.title: Meet the animals at Tierpark Hagenbeck
new.desc: Opened in 1907 and still run by the Hagenbeck family, this was the first zoo anywhere to swap cages for open enclosures separated by moats, an idea copied around the world.
new.tip: U2 stops at Hagenbecks Tierpark, right by the gate. The tropical aquarium next door is a good plan for wet days.

new.title: Float in salt water at the Kaifu-Bad
new.desc: Eimsbüttel's listed swimming baths opened in the 1890s. Besides the outdoor pools there is the Kaifu-Sole, a warm brine pool under the old hall where you float almost without effort.
new.tip: One outdoor pool is heated all year, so a winter swim under the open sky is possible. Check which areas are open before you go.

new.title: Swim in the Stadtparksee
new.desc: At the eastern end of Winterhude's Stadtpark, the lake has its own open-air lido with a beer garden beside it, a summer habit of Hamburgers for a century.
new.tip: Afterwards join the picnics and frisbee games on the great lawn. In summer there are open-air concerts on the park's Freilichtbühne.

new.title: Explore Wilhelmsburg along the Veringkanal
new.desc: Europe's largest river island is Hamburg's up-and-coming south. In the Reiherstieg quarter a canal path leads past houseboats, street art and the Honigfabrik, an old honey factory turned culture centre.
new.tip: Arrive by harbour ferry from the Landungsbrücken, then eat on Veringstraße, the neighbourhood's multicultural food street.

new.title: Circle the old Hansehafen in Stade
new.desc: Stade's tiny medieval harbour basin is ringed by half-timbered merchant houses and the Schwedenspeicher, a granary from the town's Swedish years that is now the history museum.
new.tip: The S-Bahn from Hamburg runs all the way to Stade. From the station it is a short walk across the moat into the old town.

new.title: Find the hare and the hedgehog in Buxtehude
new.desc: The Grimm tale of the race between the hare and the hedgehog is set in Buxtehude, and the town has a fountain to prove it. The old town is built around the Fleth, a canal harbour from the 1280s.
new.tip: Look for the Ewer Margareta, the last of the town's old cargo sailing boats, moored on the Fleth in front of the mill.

new.title: See the Alter Kran at Lüneburg's Stintmarkt
new.desc: Salt made Lüneburg rich, and it left through this little river port on the Ilmenau. The wooden harbour crane still stands among gabled brick houses and waterside pub terraces.
new.tip: Walk on to the square Am Sande for the finest brick gables. Regional trains from Hamburg take about half an hour.

new.title: Get off at Uelzen's Hundertwasser station
new.desc: For Expo 2000 the Austrian artist Friedensreich Hundertwasser turned an ordinary railway station into a riot of coloured columns, golden globes and wavy floors. It was one of his last projects.
new.tip: Direct regional trains from Hamburg stop here, so you step straight out into the artwork. Wander through every hall, not just the platforms.

new.title: Visit the brick cathedral on Ratzeburg's island
new.desc: Ratzeburg's old town sits on an island surrounded by four lakes, and at its green northern tip stands the Ratzeburger Dom, a mighty red-brick cathedral.
new.tip: Walk the lakeside path around the cathedral peninsula. In summer you can also hire a rail trolley and pedal the old line towards Hollenbek.

new.title: Track down Till Eulenspiegel in Mölln
new.desc: Germany's most famous prankster is said to have died of the plague in Mölln in 1350. The hilltop old town remembers him with a fountain on the market square and a memorial stone at St. Nicolai church.
new.tip: Climb the steps from the market up to the church, then walk down to the lakes that wrap around the town.

new.title: Walk the Elbstraße in Lauenburg
new.desc: Lauenburg's lower town is a single cobbled street of half-timbered skippers' houses squeezed between the Elbe and its high bank. On the Ruferplatz a bronze caller hails the passing ships.
new.tip: Check whether the museum paddle steamer Kaiser Wilhelm is sailing. For the view, climb to the old castle tower in the upper town.

new.title: Hike to the Lange Anna on Helgoland
new.desc: Germany's only high-sea island ends in a 47 metre red sandstone stack called the Lange Anna. The cliffs beside it are packed with gannets and guillemots in the breeding season.
new.tip: Follow the clifftop path around the Oberland. In season a fast catamaran sails from Hamburg's Landungsbrücken, a long but doable day trip.

new.title: Eat Matjes in Glückstadt
new.desc: This planned Danish fortress town on the Elbe, with streets fanning out from one cobbled market square, is famous for its Glückstädter Matjes: young herring matured in brine the old way.
new.tip: In mid-June the Matjeswochen open with the first barrel tapped on the market square. Trains from Hamburg run direct.

new.title: Have coffee while ships get their anthem in Wedel
new.desc: At the Schulauer Fährhaus in Wedel, every big ship entering or leaving Hamburg has been greeted since 1952. The Willkomm-Höft dips a flag and plays the national anthem of the ship's home country.
new.tip: Take the S1 to Wedel and walk down to the Elbe. Grab a terrace table at the Fährhaus and wait for the loudspeakers.

new.title: Crack Knieper claws on Helgoland
new.desc: Knieper are the claws of the brown crab, Helgoland's signature dish, eaten with your fingers and a dip. Islanders wash them down with Eiergrog, a potent hot rum and egg drink.
new.tip: Look for Knieper on menus around the harbour in the Unterland and by the colourful Hummerbuden (old lobster shacks).

new.title: Drink house-brewed beer at Mälzer in Lüneburg
new.desc: Lüneburg once had dozens of breweries. This brewhouse on Heiligengeiststraße keeps the habit alive, making its own beer on site and pouring it into stoneware mugs.
new.tip: The old Kronen brewery next door has a small brewery museum, a nice extra before or after your beer.
new.q: Mälzer Brau- und Tafelhaus, Heiligengeiststraße 43, Lüneburg

new.title: Meet wolves at Wildpark Schwarze Berge
new.desc: In the wooded hills just south of Hamburg, in Rosengarten, this wildlife park keeps bison, wolves, lynx, elk and brown bears in big natural enclosures. Pot-bellied pigs and goats wander among the visitors.
new.tip: Climb the 45 metre Elbblickturm for a view back to Blankenese and the port. It is open all year.
new.q: Wildpark Schwarze Berge, Am Wildpark 1, Rosengarten

new.title: Take a carriage into the heath from Undeloh
new.desc: The village of Undeloh lies inside the Lüneburger Heide nature reserve. The road towards the heart of the heath is closed to cars, so horse-drawn carriages wait at the edge of the village.
new.tip: The heather turns purple in August and early September. See the old heath church with its separate wooden bell tower before you set off.

new.title: Boil your own salt at the Deutsches Salzmuseum
new.desc: For a thousand years Lüneburg lived from its saltworks. The museum in the old Saline shows how the white gold was won, and lets you try making some yourself.
new.tip: Afterwards walk through the nearby Senkungsgebiet, where the salt mining made streets sag and houses lean.

new.title: Watch ships ride the lift at Scharnebeck
new.desc: Northeast of Lüneburg, two giant water-filled troughs lift whole cargo barges 38 metres up the Elbe Lateral Canal. When it opened in 1975 it was the largest ship lift in the world.
new.tip: Wait for a barge to enter and follow the whole lift from the visitor area. Excursion boats from Lauenburg sometimes ride the lift themselves.

new.title: Hike the Büsenbachtal to the Pferdekopf
new.desc: A small heath valley near Handeloh, with a stream, juniper and sandy paths, that gives you the Lüneburger Heide feeling in a short walk. The Pferdekopf hill is the lookout.
new.tip: Stay on the marked paths, as rangers watch over the reserve. It gets very busy at weekends when the heather blooms, so pick a weekday.

new.title: Pick your own apples in the Altes Land
new.desc: The Altes Land along the Elbe is northern Europe's biggest fruit orchard. At the organic Herzapfelhof Lühs in Jork you get a basket and pick apples straight from the tree.
new.tip: Apple picking runs from about mid-August into October. Sign in at the farm shop first, and borrow a hand cart if you have children along.
